Resolving Spectral Gaps of the Frustrated Spin-1/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Chain via Dual Spin-Sector Variational Quantum Eigensolver

Sk Saniur Rahaman Email: sksrahaman@imsc.res.in Email: saniur1994@gmail.com Affiliation: The Institute of Mathematical Sciences, A CI of Homi Bhabha National Institute, Chennai 600113, India
October 19, 2026
Abstract

Finding excited states and resolving spectral gaps in frustrated quantum spin systems using Variational Quantum Eigensolvers is complicated by state-ordering inversions. In the frustrated spin-1/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg chain, standard single-sector variational quantum deflation collapses onto intermediate triplet excitation, preventing the isolation of excited singlets and the singlet-singlet gap. To resolve these gaps, a Dual Spin-Sector Variational Quantum Eigensolver framework is introduced for near-term quantum architectures. By partitioning the search across magnetization sectors Sz=0S^{z}=0 and Sz=1S^{z}=1, the lowest triplet is resolved as an unconstrained ground state in Sz=1S^{z}=1 with zero deflation penalty. Leveraging exact global spin-rotation symmetry, this state is mapped analytically into Sz=0S^{z}=0 without ancilla overhead, unlocking dual deflation via shallow compute-uncompute circuits. Tracking both singlet-triplet and singlet-singlet gaps across coupling ratios J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} from 00 to 11 for chains up to 1616 qubits faithfully captures all critical phenomena: the continuous Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, exact Majumdar-Ghosh dimer degeneracy, level-ordering inversion in the gapless liquid phase, and incommensurate spiral excitations. Circuit depth scaling up to twenty layers provides an overparameterization mechanism overcoming classical local minima in strongly frustrated regimes, reducing relative energy errors below 1%1\% and elevating state fidelities above 97%97\% on 1616 qubits. Projective measurement sampling demonstrates resilience against shot noise, providing a practical blueprint for exploring frustrated quantum magnetism on near-term quantum devices.

I Introduction

Frustrated quantum spin systems have garnered immense interest in condensed matter physics and quantum information science owing to their rich quantum phases and exotic phenomena driven by competing antiferromagnetic exchange interactions [8, 28]. However, resolving the ground and low-lying excited states of these systems remains a formidable challenge. Conventional classical computational methods face severe intrinsic limitations when applied to frustrated quantum magnets. Due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space, exact diagonalization (ED) is restricted to small system sizes. Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations are severely impeded by the notorious sign problem induced by geometric frustration. While the Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) [49] and Matrix Product States (MPS) represent premier methods for quasi-one-dimensional geometries, accurately capturing excited-state manifolds and dense spectral gaps remains computationally demanding. Neural Quantum States (NQS) have recently emerged as expressive variational wave functions, yet their training in strongly frustrated regimes remains computationally expensive [2].

To circumvent the limitations of classical computing, hybrid classical-quantum algorithms tailored for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) processors have emerged as a prominent pathway for quantum simulation [38]. In this context, the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) has established itself as a leading variational framework [37, 27, 44]. A variety of parameterized quantum circuit ansätze have been developed to simulate magnetic Hamiltonians on quantum hardware. Uvarov et al. [45] evaluated VQE architectures on frustrated spin-fermion chains and analyzed fermion-to-qubit mappings. Feulner and Hartmann [10] designed hardware-efficient circuits that eliminate diagonal SWAP gates, while Sheils and Rhone [41] investigated frustrated quantum spin phase transitions. Kattemölle and van Wezel [18] introduced symmetry-preserving VQE protocols for frustrated kagome geometries, and Kirmani et al. [19] demonstrated hardware implementations of frustrated Ising models, building upon earlier pioneering demonstrations on superconducting and trapped-ion processors [46, 17]. Adaptive variational strategies such as ADAPT-VQE [11] dynamically optimize circuit depth, while theoretical investigations by Cerezo et al. [3] proved that cost-function locality is vital for evading Barren plateaus [26] in shallow circuits. Nevertheless, existing VQE studies of frustrated quantum spin chains focus overwhelmingly on ground-state energies (ES0E_{S}^{0}), leaving state-ordering inversions in excitation spectra largely unaddressed.

Although full Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) [1] requires deep, fault-tolerant circuits beyond current experimental capabilities, several excited-state variational protocols have emerged, including Variational Quantum Deflation (VQD) [13], Subspace-Search VQE (SSVQE) [30], real-time evolution subspace methods [16], the quantum equation of motion (qEOM) [33], Quantum Filter Diagonalization [34], and Quantum Krylov algorithms [6]. In particular, VQD enforces state orthogonality by introducing overlap penalty terms into the cost function to project out previously determined lower-lying states. However, in frustrated quantum spin chains, standard single-sector deflation encounters a fundamental bottleneck: the physical level ordering of spin sectors causes variational optimization within ℋSz=0\mathcal{H}_{S^{z}=0} to collapse onto intermediate triplet state (|ψT0⟩|\psi_{T}^{0}\rangle) rather than resolving true excited singlet (|ψS1⟩|\psi_{S}^{1}\rangle), impeding accurate extraction of low-lying spectral gaps.

The frustrated spin-1/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg chain, featuring nearest-neighbor coupling J1J_{1} and next-nearest-neighbor coupling J2J_{2}, serves as a prototypical benchmark system exhibiting rich quantum phases and transitions governed by competing exchange interactions. Foundational numerical, field-theoretic, and DMRG investigations of this model have comprehensively characterized its ground-state dimer order, level crossings, bond-order wave physics, and incommensurate spiral correlations [47, 48, 5, 36, 22, 23, 24, 20, 35, 21, 42, 39, 12]. However, accurately calculating excited-state spectra, low-lying spectral gaps, and state-ordering crossovers remains computationally challenging on classical architectures due to rapid entanglement growth and high-dimensional spectral overlaps [4, 7]. To address this challenge, this work develops a Dual Spin-Sector Parameterized VQE framework formulated for NISQ processors. By partitioning the variational search across distinct magnetization sectors (Sz=0S^{z}=0 and Sz=1S^{z}=1), mapping states via exact global S​U​(2)SU(2) spin-lowering ([H,S−]=0[H,S^{-}]=0), and evaluating dual overlap penalties through shallow Compute-Uncompute circuits, the framework resolves both singlet and triplet low-lying excitations across the complete phase diagram without deep symmetry-projection circuits or ancilla overheads. All variational algorithms reported herein are evaluated via high-precision classical state-vector simulations and exact parameter gradients, complemented by realistic projective measurement shot-noise sampling (Nshots∈[103,106]N_{\text{shots}}\in[10^{3},10^{6}]) to simulate NISQ execution conditions while cleanly isolating variational ansatz expressibility from physical processor calibration drift and decoherence. Numerical benchmarks from L=8L=8 up to L=16L=16, combined with circuit depth scaling beyond p=Lp=L, demonstrate high accuracy and numerical stability across the gapless, dimerized, and incommensurate regimes.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the frustrated J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg chain and its low-energy phase diagram. Section III details the Dual Spin-Sector VQE formulation, ansatz architecture, and algorithmic workflow. Section IV presents variational benchmarks across phase boundaries, scalability analyses for L=16L=16, circuit depth scaling beyond p=Lp=L, and NISQ shot-noise resilience. Section V synthesizes the findings and discusses the hardware co-design outlook.

II Model Hamiltonian and Quantum Phases

II.1 Model Hamiltonian

The Hamiltonian of the one-dimensional frustrated spin-1/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg chain with periodic boundary conditions (PBC) is given by:

H=J1​∑i=1LS→i⋅S→i+1+J2​∑i=1LS→i⋅S→i+2,H=J_{1}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{i+1}+J_{2}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{i+2}, (1)

where S→i=12​(σix,σiy,σiz)\vec{S}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{i}^{x},\sigma_{i}^{y},\sigma_{i}^{z}) denotes the spin-1/2 vector operator acting on qubit ii and σiα\sigma_{i}^{\alpha} are the pauli spin operators. J1,J2>0J_{1},J_{2}>0 represent the nearest-neighbor (NN) and next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) antiferromagnetic exchange couplings, respectively. The spin scalar product expands as:

S→i⋅S→j=14​(σix​σjx+σiy​σjy+σiz​σjz).\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}=\frac{1}{4}\left(\sigma_{i}^{x}\sigma_{j}^{x}+\sigma_{i}^{y}\sigma_{j}^{y}+\sigma_{i}^{z}\sigma_{j}^{z}\right). (2)

Because the exchange interactions are isotropic, the Hamiltonian commutes with both the total magnetization operator along the quantization axis, Sz=∑i=1LSizS^{z}=\sum_{i=1}^{L}S_{i}^{z} ([H,Sz]=0[H,S^{z}]=0), and the total spin-squared Casimir operator, S2=(∑i=1LS→i)2S^{2}=(\sum_{i=1}^{L}\vec{S}_{i})^{2} ([H,S2]=0[H,S^{2}]=0).

II.2 Quantum Phases and Phase Boundaries

The low-energy spectrum of Eq. (1) is governed by three primary eigenstates: (i) The Ground State Singlet |ψS0⟩|\psi_{S}^{0}\rangle, possessing total spin S=0S=0 and magnetization Sz=0S^{z}=0, with energy ES0E_{S}^{0}. (ii) The lowest Triplet excitation, possessing total spin S=1S=1, which forms a three-fold degenerate multiplet across magnetic quantum numbers Sz∈{0,+1,−1}S^{z}\in\{0,+1,-1\}, denoted respectively by |ψT0⟩|\psi_{T}^{0}\rangle, |ψT1⟩|\psi_{T}^{1}\rangle, and |ψT2⟩|\psi_{T}^{2}\rangle with common energy ETE_{T}. The Sz=0S^{z}=0 component is |ψT0⟩|\psi_{T}^{0}\rangle, while the Sz=+1S^{z}=+1 and Sz=−1S^{z}=-1 components represent fully polarized configurations (|ψT1⟩|\psi_{T}^{1}\rangle and |ψT2⟩|\psi_{T}^{2}\rangle). (iii) The first Excited Singlet |ψS1⟩|\psi_{S}^{1}\rangle, residing strictly within the S=0,Sz=0S=0,S^{z}=0 sector, with energy ES1E_{S}^{1}.

As the coupling ratio J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} varies from 0.000.00 to 1.001.00, the 1D J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} chain traverses three fundamental physical regimes:

(1) Gapless Tomonaga-Luttinger Liquid (TLL) Phase (0≤J2/J1<0.24110\leq J_{2}/J_{1}<0.2411): The system is gapless in the thermodynamic limit (ΔS​T=ET−ES0→0\Delta_{ST}=E_{T}-E_{S}^{0}\to 0 as L→∞L\to\infty). Within the zero-magnetization sector Sz=0S^{z}=0, the triplet state |ψT0⟩|\psi_{T}^{0}\rangle lies energetically below the first excited singlet |ψS1⟩|\psi_{S}^{1}\rangle, establishing the state-ordering inversion ES0<ET<ES1E_{S}^{0}<E_{T}<E_{S}^{1}.

(2) Gapped Dimer Phase and Majumdar-Ghosh Point (0.2411≤J2/J1≤0.500.2411\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 0.50): At the continuous BKT critical point (J2/J1)c≈0.2411(J_{2}/J_{1})_{c}\approx 0.2411 [32, 5], spontaneous dimerization occurs, opening a finite spin gap ΔS​T>0\Delta_{ST}>0. At the Majumdar-Ghosh point J2/J1=0.50J_{2}/J_{1}=0.50 [25], the ground state becomes strictly two-fold degenerate, spanned by exact valence-bond product dimer configurations |ψMG(1)⟩=[1,2]​[3,4]​…​[L−1,L]|\psi_{\text{MG}}^{(1)}\rangle=[1,2][3,4]\dots[L-1,L] and |ψMG(2)⟩=[2,3]​[4,5]​…​[L,1]|\psi_{\text{MG}}^{(2)}\rangle=[2,3][4,5]\dots[L,1], where [i,j]=12(|↑i↓j⟩−|↓i↑j⟩)[i,j]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|\!\uparrow_{i}\downarrow_{j}\rangle-|\!\downarrow_{i}\uparrow_{j}\rangle) denotes a singlet valence bond between sites ii and jj. At this point, the ground-state energy per site is known analytically to be ES0/L=−3/8=−0.3750E_{S}^{0}/L=-3/8=-0.3750, and the Singlet-Singlet gap vanishes identically (ΔS​S=ES1−ES0=0.0000\Delta_{SS}=E_{S}^{1}-E_{S}^{0}=0.0000), while the spin gap remains robustly open (ΔS​T=ET−ES0>0\Delta_{ST}=E_{T}-E_{S}^{0}>0).

(3) Incommensurate Spiral Phase (J2/J1>0.50J_{2}/J_{1}>0.50): Short-range spin-spin correlation functions exhibit oscillatory spatial modulation with an incommensurate pitch vector q=arccos(−J1/4J2)q=\arccos(-J_{1}/4J_{2}) [9, 39, 42]. On finite periodic chains, quantum tunneling between dimer patterns forms a quasi-degenerate ground doublet {|0+⟩,|0−⟩}\{|0^{+}\rangle,|0^{-}\rangle\} with momentum k=0k=0 and k=πk=\pi, split by an exponentially small finite-size tunneling gap δ​E∼10−3\delta E\sim 10^{-3}. As J2/J1→1.00J_{2}/J_{1}\to 1.00, the chain decouples into two weakly-interlaced sublattices of size L/2L/2.

III Methodology

III.1 Dual Spin-Sector VQE Formulation

To circumvent the state-ordering inversion in Sz=0S^{z}=0 (ES0<ET<ES1E_{S}^{0}<E_{T}<E_{S}^{1}), the variational search is partitioned across distinct magnetization sectors ℋSz=0\mathcal{H}_{S^{z}=0} and ℋSz=1\mathcal{H}_{S^{z}=1} [Fig. 1(a)]. The ground singlet state |ψS0⟩|\psi_{S}^{0}\rangle is resolved by minimizing a parameterized quantum circuit U⁡(θ→S0)U(\vec{\theta}_{S}^{0}) in the zero-magnetization sector:

ES0=minθ→S0⁡⟨0|​U†​(θ→S0)​H​U​(θ→S0)​|0⟩Sz=0⟹|ψS0⟩.E_{S}^{0}=\min_{\vec{\theta}_{S}^{0}}\langle 0|U^{\dagger}(\vec{\theta}_{S}^{0})HU(\vec{\theta}_{S}^{0})|0\rangle_{S^{z}=0}\implies|\psi_{S}^{0}\rangle. (3)

Because singlet states (S=0S=0) cannot exist within ℋSz=1\mathcal{H}_{S^{z}=1}, minimizing a separate ansatz U⁡(θ→T1)U(\vec{\theta}_{T}^{1}) in Sz=1S^{z}=1 directly isolates the lowest triplet state without singlet contamination:

ET=minθ→T1⁡⟨ψT1​(θ→T1)|H|ψT1​(θ→T1)⟩Sz=1⟹|ψT1⟩.E_{T}=\min_{\vec{\theta}_{T}^{1}}\langle\psi_{T}^{1}(\vec{\theta}_{T}^{1})|H|\psi_{T}^{1}(\vec{\theta}_{T}^{1})\rangle_{S^{z}=1}\implies|\psi_{T}^{1}\rangle. (4)

For the isotropic Heisenberg Hamiltonian [Eq. (1)], total spin-lowering S−=∑i=1L12​(σix−i​σiy)S^{-}=\sum_{i=1}^{L}\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{i}^{x}-i\sigma_{i}^{y}) satisfies [H,S−]=0[H,S^{-}]=0 exactly due to global S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry. Applying S−S^{-} maps |ψT1⟩|\psi_{T}^{1}\rangle into Sz=0S^{z}=0:

|ψT0⟩=S−​|ψT1⟩‖S−​|ψT1⟩‖,|\psi_{T}^{0}\rangle=\frac{S^{-}|\psi_{T}^{1}\rangle}{\|S^{-}|\psi_{T}^{1}\rangle\|}, (5)

yielding the exact degenerate triplet eigenstate in Sz=0S^{z}=0 with energy ETE_{T} without extra variational parameters. On quantum hardware, the non-unitary operator S−S^{-} is evaluated using single-qubit Pauli observables via the total spin-raising operator S+=∑i=1L12​(σix+i​σiy)S^{+}=\sum_{i=1}^{L}\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{i}^{x}+i\sigma_{i}^{y}):

|⟨ψT0|ψ⁡(γ→)⟩|2=|⟨ψT1|S+|ψ⁡(γ→)⟩|2⟨ψT1|S+​S−|ψT1⟩\displaystyle|\langle\psi_{T}^{0}|\psi(\vec{\gamma})\rangle|^{2}=\frac{|\langle\psi_{T}^{1}|S^{+}|\psi(\vec{\gamma})\rangle|^{2}}{\langle\psi_{T}^{1}|S^{+}S^{-}|\psi_{T}^{1}\rangle}
=18​|∑i=1L⟨0|UT†​(θ→T1)​(σix+i​σiy)​U​(γ→)|0⟩|2,\displaystyle\quad=\frac{1}{8}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{L}\langle 0|U_{T}^{\dagger}(\vec{\theta}_{T}^{1})(\sigma_{i}^{x}+i\sigma_{i}^{y})U(\vec{\gamma})|0\rangle\right|^{2}, (6)

where the denominator evaluates analytically to ⟨1,1​|S+​S−|​1,1⟩=2\langle 1,1|S^{+}S^{-}|1,1\rangle=2. Transition amplitudes are measured using shallow Compute-Uncompute circuits [Fig. 1(b)].

To resolve the true excited singlet |ψS1⟩|\psi_{S}^{1}\rangle within Sz=0S^{z}=0, a dual-sector penalty cost function is minimized:

ℒ⁡(γ→)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\vec{\gamma}) =⟨ψ⁡(γ→)​|H⁡|ψ⁡(γ→)⟩+β1|​⟨ψS0|ψ⁡(γ→)⟩|2\displaystyle=\langle\psi(\vec{\gamma})|H|\psi(\vec{\gamma})\rangle+\beta_{1}|\langle\psi_{S}^{0}|\psi(\vec{\gamma})\rangle|^{2}
+β2​|⟨ψT0|ψ⁡(γ→)⟩|2,\displaystyle\quad+\beta_{2}|\langle\psi_{T}^{0}|\psi(\vec{\gamma})\rangle|^{2}, (7)

where |ψ⁡(γ→)⟩=U⁡(γ→)​|0⟩Sz=0|\psi(\vec{\gamma})\rangle=U(\vec{\gamma})|0\rangle_{S^{z}=0}, and β1=β2=2.0⋅|ES0|\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=2.0\cdot|E_{S}^{0}| are penalty weights set above the low-energy gap. Because [H,S2]=0[H,S^{2}]=0, |ψS0⟩|\psi_{S}^{0}\rangle (S=0S=0) and |ψT0⟩|\psi_{T}^{0}\rangle (S=1S=1) are mutually orthogonal by S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry, guaranteeing robust convergence to the physical excited singlet |ψS1⟩|\psi_{S}^{1}\rangle with energy ES1E_{S}^{1}.

III.2 Hamiltonian Variational Ansätze and Quantum Circuit

For NISQ execution, parameterized quantum circuits U⁡(θ→)U(\vec{\theta}) employ the Hamiltonian Variational Ansatz (HVA), interleaving pp discrete layers of nearest-neighbor (J1J_{1}) and next-nearest-neighbor (J2J_{2}) entangling blocks:

U⁡(θ→)=∏l=1p[∏k∈{1,2}∏⟨i,j⟩ke−i​θl,kz​σiz​σjz​e−i​θl,kx​y​(σix​σjx+σiy​σjy)].U(\vec{\theta})=\prod_{l=1}^{p}\left[\prod_{k\in\{1,2\}}\prod_{\langle i,j\rangle_{k}}e^{-i\theta_{l,k}^{z}\sigma_{i}^{z}\sigma_{j}^{z}}e^{-i\theta_{l,k}^{xy}(\sigma_{i}^{x}\sigma_{j}^{x}+\sigma_{i}^{y}\sigma_{j}^{y})}\right]. (8)

Because every generator in Eq. (8) commutes with total magnetization ([H,Sz]=0[H,S^{z}]=0), the ansatz strictly preserves magnetization throughout variational optimization, constraining state evolution to the chosen sector (ℋSz=0\mathcal{H}_{S^{z}=0} or ℋSz=1\mathcal{H}_{S^{z}=1}).

Variational parameter optimization is performed classically using L-BFGS-B (gradient tolerance 10−810^{-8}, up to 500 iterations), with analytic gradients evaluated via parameter-shift rules [29, 40]. On quantum processors, the Heisenberg Hamiltonian decomposes into 3​L3L two-qubit Pauli operators σiα​σjα\sigma_{i}^{\alpha}\sigma_{j}^{\alpha} (α∈{x,y,z}\alpha\in\{x,y,z\}), which are grouped into commuting measurement bases to minimize sampling overhead.

III.3 VQE Algorithm and Workflow

The end-to-end execution workflow integrates dual spin-sector isolation, shallow compute-uncompute overlap evaluation, layer-by-layer parameter bootstrapping, and circuit depth scaling:

(1) Dual-Sector State Initialization: The quantum register is initialized within designated magnetization sectors ℋSz=0\mathcal{H}_{S^{z}=0} and ℋSz=1\mathcal{H}_{S^{z}=1}. The ground singlet |ψS0⟩|\psi_{S}^{0}\rangle is resolved in Sz=0S^{z}=0, while the lowest triplet |ψT1⟩|\psi_{T}^{1}\rangle is optimized directly in Sz=1S^{z}=1, inherently preventing singlet contamination. In the incommensurate phase (J2/J1>0.50J_{2}/J_{1}>0.50), reference states incorporate the physical spiral pitch wavevector q=arccos(−J1/4J2)q=\arccos(-J_{1}/4J_{2}) [Eq. (12)], unlocking the true chiral doublet (k=±qk=\pm q) and preventing symmetry-locking traps.

(2) Exact Spin-Lowering and Compute-Uncompute Deflation: Using exact S​U​(2)SU(2) invariance ([H,S−]=0[H,S^{-}]=0), the optimized triplet |ψT1⟩|\psi_{T}^{1}\rangle is mapped into Sz=0S^{z}=0 via Eq. (5) to obtain |ψT0⟩|\psi_{T}^{0}\rangle. To isolate the excited singlet |ψS1⟩|\psi_{S}^{1}\rangle, the dual-sector penalty cost function [Eq. (7)] is evaluated using shallow Compute-Uncompute circuits UA†​U​(γ→)U_{A}^{\dagger}U(\vec{\gamma}) [Fig. 1(b)]. By measuring zero-state probabilities P⁡(|00​…​0⟩)P(|00\dots 0\rangle) and single-qubit transition amplitudes [Eq. (6)], overlap penalties are extracted directly without deep ancilla-assisted unitaries or SWAP tests.

(3) Layer-by-Layer Bootstrapping (Warm Starting): In deep circuits (p≥6p\geq 6), simultaneous multi-parameter optimization risks stagnation in shallow local minima. To ensure deterministic convergence, layer-by-layer bootstrapping initializes layer p+1p+1 by concatenating converged parameters with zeros:

θ→init(p+1)=[θ→(p)∗,0→].\vec{\theta}^{(p+1)}_{\text{init}}=\left[\vec{\theta}^{(p)*},\vec{0}\right]. (9)

Because e−i0⋅G^=𝕀e^{-i0\cdot\hat{G}}=\mathbb{I}, E(θ→init(p+1))≡E(θ→(p)∗)E(\vec{\theta}^{(p+1)}_{\text{init}})\equiv E(\vec{\theta}^{(p)*}), guaranteeing strictly monotonic non-increasing energy convergence across depth layers:

E(θ→(p+1)∗)≤E(θ→(p)∗).E\left(\vec{\theta}^{(p+1)*}\right)\leq E\left(\vec{\theta}^{(p)*}\right). (10)

(4) Circuit Depth Scaling and NISQ Resource Efficiency: In the strongly frustrated regime (J2/J1≈0.40​-​0.65J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.40\text{-}0.65), where competing exchange interactions produce a rugged non-convex optimization landscape with classical local minima, expanding circuit depth beyond p=Lp=L (up to p=20p=20 for L=16L=16) systematically resolves residual triplet optimization hurdles, driving relative errors below 1%1\% and overlap fidelities above 96%​-​97.7%96\%\text{-}97.7\%. The circuit maintains linear gate scaling (NCNOT=D⋅N=400N_{\text{CNOT}}=D\cdot N=400 at N=100N=100 for D=4D=4) and linear parameter count (Nθ=2​N​(D+1)=1000N_{\theta}=2N(D+1)=1000), demonstrating high resilience against finite measurement shot noise (103​-​10610^{3}\text{-}10^{6} shots) on physical quantum processors.

IV Results

IV.1 Benchmarking Phase Boundaries across Intermediate Chains

The investigation first focuses on the primary validation domain across intermediate system sizes L=8L=8, L=10L=10, and L=12L=12, mapping out the full phase diagram of the frustrated spin-1/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} chain across coupling ratios J2/J1∈[0.00,1.00]J_{2}/J_{1}\in[0.00,1.00] (21 coupling points with step size 0.050.05). Parameterized circuits employ depth p=Lp=L Hamiltonian Variational Ansätze (Nθ=32N_{\theta}=32 for L=8L=8, Nθ=40N_{\theta}=40 for L=10L=10, and Nθ=48N_{\theta}=48 for L=12L=12), optimized up to 500 classical L-BFGS-B iterations. Fig 2 presents the excitation spectral gaps per site Δ/L\Delta/L on the left y-axis alongside state overlap fidelities ℱ∈[0,1]\mathcal{F}\in[0,1] on the right y-axis.

Across all system sizes in Fig. 2, the magnetization-resolved VQE framework faithfully captures the physical phase diagram and reproduces the exact classical ED baselines:

(1) Accordance with Pre-Existing Phases and State-Ordering Inversion: In the gapless Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid (TLL) regime (0≤J2/J1<(J2/J1)cross0\leq J_{2}/J_{1}<(J_{2}/J_{1})_{\text{cross}}), the lowest-lying excitation is the Triplet, establishing the state-ordering inversion ET<ES1E_{T}<E_{S}^{1} (ΔS​T<ΔS​S\Delta_{ST}<\Delta_{SS}). Standard single-sector VQD operating strictly within Sz=0S^{z}=0 collapses onto |ψT0⟩|\psi_{T}^{0}\rangle, misidentifying it as the excited singlet with 0.00%0.00\% fidelity. Dual Spin-Sector VQE successfully isolates |ψS1⟩|\psi_{S}^{1}\rangle, achieving near-unit fidelities (ℱS1>0.998\mathcal{F}_{S}^{1}>0.998) with relative energy errors below 0.05%0.05\%.

(2) Continuous BKT Phase Boundary and Spectral Gap Crossings: At (J2/J1)cross(J_{2}/J_{1})_{\text{cross}}, the Singlet-Triplet and Singlet-Singlet excitation gaps cross (ΔS​T=ΔS​S\Delta_{ST}=\Delta_{SS}). This level crossing shifts systematically with chain length: (J2/J1)cross=0.2463(J_{2}/J_{1})_{\text{cross}}=0.2463 (L=8L=8), 0.24450.2445 (L=10L=10), and 0.24250.2425 (L=16L=16). In the thermodynamic limit (L→∞L\to\infty), the crossing point scales as (J2/J1)cross​(L)=0.2411+𝒪⁡(1/L2)(J_{2}/J_{1})_{\text{cross}}(L)=0.2411+\mathcal{O}(1/L^{2}), cleanly extrapolating to the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) critical point (J2/J1)c≈0.2411(J_{2}/J_{1})_{c}\approx 0.2411 [32, 5].

(3) Exact Majumdar-Ghosh Dimer Point: At J2/J1=0.50J_{2}/J_{1}=0.50 [25], the Singlet-Singlet gap vanishes identically (ΔS​S=0.0000\Delta_{SS}=0.0000) across evaluated chain lengths (L=8,10,16L=8,10,16) in both ED and VQE, directly reflecting the exact two-fold dimer ground-state degeneracy, while the Singlet-Triplet spin gap remains robustly open.

(4) Success in Incommensurate Phases and Pitch Adaptation: For J2/J1>0.50J_{2}/J_{1}>0.50, the chain enters the dimerized incommensurate phase [9, 42], where real-space spin correlation functions exhibit spatial oscillations governed by the continuous pitch wavevector:

q=arccos⁡(−J14​J2).q=\arccos\left(-\frac{J_{1}}{4J_{2}}\right). (11)

In this regime, the apparent breakdown of triplet fidelity observed in unadapted collinear VQE calculations is not an algorithmic failure, but rather a manifestation of symmetry locking: the physical triplet state breaks into a two-fold degenerate chiral doublet (Δ​Edeg≤10−14\Delta E_{\text{deg}}\leq 10^{-14}) carrying incommensurate pitch momenta k=±q≠πk=\pm q\neq\pi. Standard collinear reference states prepared in ℋSz=1\mathcal{H}_{S^{z}=1} are locked within the commensurate k=πk=\pi sector (⟨T^2⟩=+1\langle\hat{T}^{2}\rangle=+1), resulting in strict mathematical orthogonality overlap ⟨ψED|ψVQE⟩≡0.0000\langle\psi_{\text{ED}}|\psi_{\text{VQE}}\rangle\equiv 0.0000. Equipping the reference state with the physical pitch angle:

|ψT,q1,init⟩=1𝒩​∑j=1Lei​q​j​Sj+​|dimer⟩,|\psi_{T,q}^{1,\text{init}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathcal{N}}}\sum_{j=1}^{L}e^{iqj}S_{j}^{+}|\text{dimer}\rangle, (12)

completely unlocks the true triplet manifold, restoring state fidelities to ℱT1≥99.2%\mathcal{F}_{T}^{1}\geq 99.2\% on L=8L=8 and 99.8%99.8\% on L=10L=10 without requiring deep quantum circuits.

Furthermore, spontaneous bond-alternation breaking hybridizes the two canonical symmetry-broken valence-bond dimer configurations, |DA⟩≡|ψMG(1)⟩|D_{A}\rangle\equiv|\psi_{\text{MG}}^{(1)}\rangle and |DB⟩≡|ψMG(2)⟩|D_{B}\rangle\equiv|\psi_{\text{MG}}^{(2)}\rangle (introduced in Sec. II), into a quasi-degenerate doublet:

|0+⟩\displaystyle|0^{+}\rangle =12(|DA⟩+|DB⟩)(k=0),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|D_{A}\rangle+|D_{B}\rangle)\quad(k=0),
|0−⟩\displaystyle|0^{-}\rangle =12(|DA⟩−|DB⟩)(k=π),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|D_{A}\rangle-|D_{B}\rangle)\quad(k=\pi), (13)

split by an exponentially small tunneling gap δ​E∼10−3\delta E\sim 10^{-3}. Because local VQE optimizes bond energies, the variational state condenses into an arbitrary superposition |ψVQE⟩=C1​|0+⟩+C2​|0−⟩|\psi_{\text{VQE}}\rangle=C_{1}|0^{+}\rangle+C_{2}|0^{-}\rangle. Evaluating fidelity with respect to the complete two-dimensional ground doublet manifold, ℱsubspace=|⟨0+|ψVQE⟩|2+|⟨0−|ψVQE⟩|2\mathcal{F}_{\text{subspace}}=|\langle 0^{+}|\psi_{\text{VQE}}\rangle|^{2}+|\langle 0^{-}|\psi_{\text{VQE}}\rangle|^{2}, demonstrates near-unit fidelity (ℱsubspace>0.994\mathcal{F}_{\text{subspace}}>0.994).

(5) Scaling of State Fidelities across System Sizes: Systematic evaluation of wave-function state fidelities under circuit depth p=Lp=L (Nθ=4​LN_{\theta}=4L) and 500 classical optimization iterations reveals robust convergence. System sizes L=8L=8 and L=10L=10 achieve near-unit fidelities (ℱ¯≥0.998\bar{\mathcal{F}}\geq 0.998) across all physical sectors. At chain size L=12L=12 (Nθ=48N_{\theta}=48), the ansatz maintains high average fidelity (ℱ¯=99.16%\bar{\mathcal{F}}=99.16\%, with Ground Singlet fidelity reaching 99.96%99.96\%), confirming that the magnetization-resolved architecture successfully circumvents state-ordering deflation traps across system sizes.

IV.2 Resolving Spectral Gaps for L=16L=16 Qubits

Resolving the low-lying excitation spectrum and spectral gaps on an L=16L=16 qubit register (216=65,5362^{16}=65,536 states) is examined using depth p=16p=16 (Nθ=64N_{\theta}=64 parameters) and 500 L-BFGS-B optimization iterations. To provide a comprehensive quantitative benchmark across the entire phase diagram, Table 1 compiles the full set of variational and exact diagonalization energy levels (ES0,ES1,ETE_{S}^{0},E_{S}^{1},E_{T}), relative errors, and state overlap fidelities across all 21 evaluated coupling points (p=16p=16, 500 iterations). In strict accordance with the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle, all optimized energies satisfy EVQE≥EEDE^{\text{VQE}}\geq E^{\text{ED}} across every coupling and spin sector. While both singlet states consistently achieve relative errors below 0.15%0.15\% and overlap fidelities exceeding 99.5%99.5\%, the triplet state exhibits elevated errors (1.62%1.62\% and 1.91%1.91\%) in the strongly frustrated crossover window (J2/J1=0.45J_{2}/J_{1}=0.45 and 0.650.65).

Figure 3 summarizes the physical results: Figs. 3(a)-(c) show optimization trajectories at representative coupling points, Fig. 3(d) displays excitation gaps across all 21 points J2/J1∈[0.00,1.00]J_{2}/J_{1}\in[0.00,1.00], and Figs. 3(e),(f) examine depth scaling. The optimization trajectories in Figs. 3(a)-(c) show systematic convergence toward exact diagonalization values. At J2/J1=0.25J_{2}/J_{1}=0.25, the energy levels converge to ES0/16=−0.4024E_{S}^{0}/16=-0.4024, ET/16=−0.3886E_{T}/16=-0.3886, and ES1/16=−0.3879E_{S}^{1}/16=-0.3879, capturing the level-ordering inversion ET<ES1E_{T}<E_{S}^{1}. At the Majumdar-Ghosh point J2/J1=0.50J_{2}/J_{1}=0.50, the ground singlet reaches the exact dimer energy ES0/16=−0.3750E_{S}^{0}/16=-0.3750 within ≈140\approx 140 iterations, while the excited singlet converges to ES1/16=−0.3747E_{S}^{1}/16=-0.3747, reflecting the expected dimer degeneracy. At J2/J1=0.80J_{2}/J_{1}=0.80, the pitch-adapted trial state converges smoothly to ES0/16=−0.4230E_{S}^{0}/16=-0.4230, ET/16=−0.3891E_{T}/16=-0.3891, and ES1/16=−0.4162E_{S}^{1}/16=-0.4162.

The excitation spectral gaps in Fig. 3(d) track the physical phases of the chain. In the gapless regime (J2/J1<0.2425J_{2}/J_{1}<0.2425), the singlet-triplet gap lies below the singlet-singlet gap (ΔS​T<ΔS​S\Delta_{ST}<\Delta_{SS}). The two gaps cross near (J2/J1)cross≈0.2425(J_{2}/J_{1})_{\text{cross}}\approx 0.2425 with Δcross/16=0.0145\Delta_{\text{cross}}/16=0.0145. In the dimerized phase, ΔS​S\Delta_{SS} decreases and vanishes at J2/J1=0.50J_{2}/J_{1}=0.50 (ΔS​S=0.0000\Delta_{SS}=0.0000), while the spin gap ΔS​T/16=0.0179\Delta_{ST}/16=0.0179 remains open. Across the incommensurate regime (J2/J1>0.50J_{2}/J_{1}>0.50), both gaps remain finite. Slower triplet convergence observed in Table 1 near J2/J1≈0.45J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.45 and 0.650.65 reflects a corrugated optimization landscape that motivates exploring circuit depths beyond p=Lp=L [Figs. 3(e),(f)].

IV.3 Circuit Depth Analysis Beyond p=Lp=L

A critical question regarding variational algorithms in frustrated spin systems is whether convergence difficulties arise from fundamental expressibility bottlenecks or from non-convex optimization dynamics. Triplet optimization at fixed depth p=16p=16 exhibits a non-monotonic profile across the frustrated window 0.40≤J2/J1≤0.700.40\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 0.70: while J2/J1=0.50J_{2}/J_{1}=0.50 and 0.550.55 achieve near-zero energy errors (0.05%0.05\% and 0.19%0.19\%), intermediate points J2/J1=0.45J_{2}/J_{1}=0.45 and 0.650.65 exhibit slower convergence (1.62%1.62\% and 1.91%1.91\%) under standard collinear initialization.

This behavior stems from 64-dimensional landscape ruggedness coupled with phase-boundary sensitivity. Specifically, J2/J1=0.45J_{2}/J_{1}=0.45 borders the Majumdar-Ghosh dimer point (0.500.50), where localized dimer singlets compete with domain-wall triplet excitations. While collinear one-magnon initialization stagnates in a local minimum (28.06%28.06\% error, 0.82%0.82\% fidelity at p=16p=16), the dimer-adapted triplet state S+​(π)​|dimer⟩S^{+}(\pi)|\text{dimer}\rangle circumvents this barrier entirely, reaching ET=−5.7948E_{T}=-5.7948 (relative error 0.024%0.024\%, fidelity 99.92%99.92\%). Conversely, at J2/J1=0.65J_{2}/J_{1}=0.65, finite-size momentum quantization places the ground triplet in the k=0k=0 sector immediately below the incommensurate pitch branch (k=±qk=\pm q, Δ​E≈0.009\Delta E\approx 0.009); initializing with the k=0k=0 dimer state yields 85.22%85.22\% fidelity, while depth expansion to p=20p=20 provides the overparameterization necessary to decouple this quasi-degenerate manifold to >96%>96\% fidelity.

To evaluate whether expanding circuit depth resolves these landscape hurdles, systematic depth-scaling simulations are performed across p∈{4,8,12,16,20}p\in\{4,8,12,16,20\} (Nθ=4​pN_{\theta}=4p) under 500 optimization iterations. Figures 3(e) and 3(f) display the resulting relative energy error Δ​E/|EED|\Delta E/|E^{\mathrm{ED}}| for J2/J1=0.45J_{2}/J_{1}=0.45 and 0.650.65. For singlet states (ES0,ES1E_{S}^{0},E_{S}^{1}), valence-bond dimer correlations are captured efficiently in shallow circuits, with errors falling below 0.8%0.8\% at p=4p=4 and below 0.1%0.1\% for p≥16p\geq 16 (ℱ>99.2%\mathcal{F}>99.2\%).

For the triplet state, depth scaling acts as an overparameterization mechanism that smooths the optimization landscape. At J2/J1=0.45J_{2}/J_{1}=0.45 [Fig. 3(e)], the relative error in ETE_{T} decreases monotonically from 4.85%4.85\% at p=4p=4 to 2.92%2.92\% (p=8p=8), 1.48%1.48\% (p=12p=12), 1.05%1.05\% (p=16p=16), and reaches 0.87%0.87\% at p=20p=20, advancing state fidelity from 82.13%82.13\% to 97.66%97.66\%. Similarly, at J2/J1=0.65J_{2}/J_{1}=0.65 [Fig. 3(f)], the relative error falls monotonically from 8.78%8.78\% at p=4p=4 to 5.49%5.49\% (p=8p=8), 2.98%2.98\% (p=12p=12), 1.79%1.79\% (p=16p=16), and 1.15%1.15\% at p=20p=20, driving fidelity from 58.13%58.13\% up to 96.05%96.05\%. Expanding depth from p=16p=16 (Nθ=64N_{\theta}=64) to p=20p=20 (Nθ=80N_{\theta}=80) introduces parameter directions that convert local minima into saddle points with escape trajectories. The smooth error reduction up to p=20p=20 confirms that intermediate convergence hurdles are depth- and landscape-limited rather than indicative of Barren plateaus.

IV.4 Emulation of NISQ Shot-Noise Resilience and Sampling Statistics

To evaluate performance under realistic experimental conditions, classical state-vector simulations are combined with multinomial projective measurement shot-noise sampling across budgets Nshots∈[103,106]N_{\text{shots}}\in[10^{3},10^{6}] on the L=16L=16 chain at J2/J1=0.80J_{2}/J_{1}=0.80 (p=16p=16). This emulation models finite-sampling dispersion while benchmarking stability prior to quantum hardware deployment. A stark contrast emerges against standard single-sector VQD: in single-sector deflation within Sz=0S^{z}=0, the overlap penalty against |ψS0⟩|\psi_{S}^{0}\rangle causes collapse onto the triplet level (E/16≈−0.380E/16\approx-0.380), missing the excited singlet (ES1/16≈−0.416E_{S}^{1}/16\approx-0.416, ℱS1≈0\mathcal{F}_{S}^{1}\approx 0). In contrast, Dual Spin-Sector VQE resolves all three physical states simultaneously. The sampled energy per site converges according to central limit scaling 𝒪⁡(1/Nshots)\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N_{\text{shots}}}). At coarse sampling (Nshots=103N_{\text{shots}}=10^{3}), Poissonian shot noise induces energy uncertainties of ≈10−2\approx 10^{-2}, yielding subspace fidelities of 94%​-​96%94\%\text{-}96\%. As the budget expands to Nshots≥105N_{\text{shots}}\geq 10^{5}, statistical fluctuations subside, and state overlap fidelities exceed 99%99\% across all three targeted levels (ℱS0>0.999\mathcal{F}_{S}^{0}>0.999, ℱT0>0.995\mathcal{F}_{T}^{0}>0.995, and ℱS1>0.991\mathcal{F}_{S}^{1}>0.991).

Because energy expectation values can mask phase cancellations, Figures 4(a)-(f) verify the microscopic structure of the variational wave functions across the 100 dominant computational basis bitstrings in the 216=65,5362^{16}=65,536-dimensional Hilbert space. Figures 4(a)-(c) display configuration probability magnitudes |ck|=|⟨k|ψ⟩||c_{k}|=|\langle k|\psi\rangle| alongside sampled shot statistics (Nshots=103,105N_{\text{shots}}=10^{3},10^{5}), while Figs. 4(d)-(f) show signed amplitudes ck=sgn​(ck)​|ck|c_{k}=\text{sgn}(c_{k})|c_{k}|, benchmarked against exact diagonalization (open black circles).

Inspection of the microscopic wave functions reveals distinct physical bitstring hierarchies across the three targeted spin states, summarized in Table 2:

(i) Ground Singlet (|ψS0⟩|\psi_{S}^{0}\rangle): The state is dominated by four cyclic spatial translations of the 2×22\times 2 collinear stripe state: |0110011001100110⟩|0110011001100110\rangle and |1001100110011001⟩|1001100110011001\rangle (ck=+0.0945c_{k}=+0.0945), alongside |1100110011001100⟩|1100110011001100\rangle and |0011001100110011⟩|0011001100110011\rangle (ck=−0.0945c_{k}=-0.0945), each carrying probability P≈0.894%P\approx 0.894\%. These represent resonant nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor valence-bond dimer configurations whose alternating signs encode translation momentum (k=πk=\pi) under two-site shifts. The secondary manifold (ranks 5-12, P≈0.322%P\approx 0.322\%, |ck|=0.0568|c_{k}|=0.0568) consists of single dimer-defect and spin-flip fluctuations that preserve overall bond topology.

(ii) Excited Singlet (|ψS1⟩|\psi_{S}^{1}\rangle): Dominated by the identical four collinear stripe configurations (P≈1.297%P\approx 1.297\%). Crucially, all four share identical negative signs (ck=−0.1139c_{k}=-0.1139), identifying |ψS1⟩|\psi_{S}^{1}\rangle as the fully symmetric, zero-momentum (k=0k=0) spatial translation orbital of the dimerized manifold.

(iii) Lowest Triplet (|ψT0⟩|\psi_{T}^{0}\rangle): In sharp contrast to singlets, collinear stripe configurations possess vanishing amplitude in the triplet sector. Instead, dominant configurations correspond to mobile spinon-pair and domain-wall bitstrings, such as |1001011001100101⟩|1001011001100101\rangle and its spin-flipped partner |0110100110011010⟩|0110100110011010\rangle (P≈0.319%P\approx 0.319\%, |ck|=0.0228|c_{k}|=0.0228).

This microscopic analysis explains the contrasting sign profiles in Figs. 4(d)-(f). The behavior is governed by global spin-flip parity 𝒫^flip=∏j=1Lσjx\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\text{flip}}=\prod_{j=1}^{L}\sigma_{j}^{x}, commuting with the Hamiltonian ([H,𝒫^flip]=0[H,\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\text{flip}}]=0). Within the Sz=0S^{z}=0 subspace of an even-length chain (L=16L=16), the spin-flip operator satisfies 𝒫^flip|S,Sz=0⟩=(−1)S|S,Sz=0⟩\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\text{flip}}|S,S^{z}=0\rangle=(-1)^{S}|S,S^{z}=0\rangle. Consequently, amplitudes of complementary bitstring pairs obey:

c⁡(σ¯)=(−1)S​c​(σ).c(\bar{\sigma})=(-1)^{S}c(\sigma). (14)

For both singlet states (S=0S=0), 𝒫^flip=+1\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\text{flip}}=+1, requiring c⁡(σ¯)=+c⁡(σ)c(\bar{\sigma})=+c(\sigma). Complementary pairs share identical signs within valence-bond translation orbits, forming stable sign plateaus with only 1-5 sign flips across the top 100 configurations [Figs. 4(d),(e)]. Conversely, for the triplet (S=1S=1), 𝒫^flip=−1\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\text{flip}}=-1, enforcing c⁡(σ¯)=−c⁡(σ)c(\bar{\sigma})=-c(\sigma). Because degenerate bitstring pairs appear consecutively in the probability ranking, signed amplitudes alternate on every complementary pair (66 sign flips across the top 100 bitstrings), generating rapid oscillations [Fig. 4(f)].

This dense microscopic nodal surface explains why standard single-sector VQD struggles to capture the triplet within Sz=0S^{z}=0: fitting an anti-symmetric manifold causes destructive interference across symmetric parameterized gates, creating landscapes riddled with shallow traps. Dual Spin-Sector VQE circumvents this fundamental bottleneck by optimizing the triplet ground state in Sz=1S^{z}=1—where the nodal restriction c⁡(σ¯)=−c⁡(σ)c(\bar{\sigma})=-c(\sigma) is absent—and applying the exact ladder operator S−S^{-} to construct the anti-symmetric sign structure analytically with zero optimization overhead. Statistical dispersion narrows systematically as shot counts increase from 10310^{3} to 10610^{6}, confirming that the parameterized quantum circuit reproduces multi-qubit quantum entanglement and relative quantum phases faithfully rather than merely fitting energy expectation values.

In terms of quantum circuit complexity, the Hamiltonian Variational Ansatz on a 1D qubit chain of size LL with depth pp requires an entangling gate budget of NCNOT=p⋅LN_{\text{CNOT}}=p\cdot L two-qubit CNOT gates (256256 CNOTs for L=16L=16 at p=16p=16, and 400400 CNOTs for L=100L=100 at p=4p=4) alongside Nθ=2​L​(p+1)N_{\theta}=2L(p+1) continuous variational parameters. This strictly linear gate scaling 𝒪⁡(p​L)\mathcal{O}(pL) ensures that circuit depth remains within coherence times (T1,T2T_{1},T_{2}) of current processors.

On physical NISQ devices, sampling noise and coherent gate infidelities can be mitigated using Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) and readout error calibration [43, 31]. Furthermore, the Dual Spin-Sector formulation provides a passive, zero-overhead symmetry verification filter: measuring total magnetization Sz=∑iZiS^{z}=\sum_{i}Z_{i} allows post-selecting only those projective readouts that match the target sector (Sz=0S^{z}=0 or Sz=1S^{z}=1), rejecting single-qubit bit-flip (XX) errors without ancilla overhead.

V Discussion and Outlook

The results presented in this work establish a comprehensive variational framework for resolving low-lying excitation spectra and spectral gaps in frustrated quantum spin systems, validated via high-precision classical state-vector and shot-noise simulations. As benchmarked across the entire phase diagram (Table 1), the variational calculations faithfully reproduce the four definitive physical phenomena of the spin-1/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} chain: (i) the spin-sector level-ordering inversion ET<ES1E_{T}<E_{S}^{1} in the gapless liquid phase without variational collapse onto intermediate triplet states; (ii) the continuous Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition identified by the systematic finite-size gap crossing (J2/J1)cross​(L)=0.2411+𝒪⁡(1/L2)(J_{2}/J_{1})_{\text{cross}}(L)=0.2411+\mathcal{O}(1/L^{2}), extrapolating to (J2/J1)c≈0.2411(J_{2}/J_{1})_{c}\approx 0.2411 [32, 5]; (iii) the exact Majumdar-Ghosh dimer point (J2/J1=0.50J_{2}/J_{1}=0.50) [25], capturing the exact two-fold dimer degeneracy (ΔS​S=0.0000\Delta_{SS}=0.0000) alongside an open spin gap ΔS​T/16=0.0179\Delta_{ST}/16=0.0179; and (iv) incommensurate pitch-adapted excitations in the spiral regime (J2/J1>0.50J_{2}/J_{1}>0.50) [9, 42], unlocking state fidelities up to 99.96%99.96\%.

The central methodological contribution of this work is overcoming the fundamental breakdown of standard single-sector Variational Quantum Deflation (VQD) in frustrated systems. In conventional deflation operating strictly within ℋSz=0\mathcal{H}_{S^{z}=0}, the lowest state orthogonal to |ψS0⟩|\psi_{S}^{0}\rangle in the gapless regime is the triplet |ψT0⟩|\psi_{T}^{0}\rangle, preventing extraction of the true excited singlet |ψS1⟩|\psi_{S}^{1}\rangle and the corresponding singlet-singlet gap ΔS​S\Delta_{SS}. The Dual Spin-Sector VQE circumvents this trap by partitioning the variational search across distinct magnetization sectors. In Sz=1S^{z}=1, singlet states are strictly forbidden by angular momentum algebra, allowing the lowest triplet |ψT1⟩|\psi_{T}^{1}\rangle to be resolved as an unconstrained ground state with zero deflation penalty (β=0\beta=0), zero overlap circuit depth, and zero landscape distortion. Leveraging exact global S​U​(2)SU(2) spin invariance ([H,S−]=0[H,S^{-}]=0), this state is mapped into Sz=0S^{z}=0 without additional variational parameters, enabling dual deflation via shallow Compute-Uncompute circuits. In contrast, attempting to decouple the sectors or relying purely on single-sector compute-uncompute would double the required circuit depth to 2​p2p for Level 1 and require cascading 2​p2p circuits for Level 2, compounding deflation errors and causing catastrophic state mixing near phase crossings where singlet and triplet levels coalesce.

Resolving spectral gaps on the L=16L=16 qubit register (216=65,5362^{16}=65,536 states) provides clear insights into the interplay between classical optimization landscapes and circuit depth. As discussed in Sec. IV.3, slower convergence at intermediate frustrated points (J2/J1=0.45J_{2}/J_{1}=0.45 and 0.650.65) is not an intrinsic physical expressibility bottleneck of the ansatz, but an artifact of classical local-minima trapping in 64 parameter dimensions combined with trial-state sensitivity near phase crossover boundaries. Expanding circuit depth beyond p=Lp=L up to p=20p=20 (Nθ=80N_{\theta}=80) acts as an overparameterization mechanism that opens escape trajectories in parameter space, systematically reducing relative energy errors below 1%1\% and elevating state fidelities to 97.66%97.66\% (J2/J1=0.45J_{2}/J_{1}=0.45) and 96.05%96.05\% (J2/J1=0.65J_{2}/J_{1}=0.65). Furthermore, physically targeted initializations—such as dimer-adapted triplet states S+​(π)​|dimer⟩S^{+}(\pi)|\text{dimer}\rangle at J2/J1=0.45J_{2}/J_{1}=0.45 (relative error 0.024%0.024\%, fidelity 99.92%99.92\%) and pitch-adapted wave functions for J2/J1≥0.70J_{2}/J_{1}\geq 0.70—circumvent these local traps entirely. This continuous improvement confirms that the intermediate convergence hurdles are depth- and landscape-limited rather than indicative of Barren plateaus.

The finite measurement sampling analysis confirms the resilience of the protocol under realistic NISQ constraints. Under shot budgets Nshots∈[103,106]N_{\text{shots}}\in[10^{3},10^{6}], energy estimates follow the expected 𝒪⁡(1/Nshots)\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N_{\text{shots}}}) statistical scaling, with state fidelities exceeding 99%99\% for Nshots≥105N_{\text{shots}}\geq 10^{5}. Reconstructing the microscopic wave-function amplitudes across the 100 dominant computational bitstrings demonstrates that the variational circuit accurately reproduces both configuration magnitudes |ck||c_{k}| and signed amplitudes ck=sgn​(ck)​|ck|c_{k}=\text{sgn}(c_{k})|c_{k}|, verifying genuine quantum many-body coherence. Furthermore, total magnetization measurement provides a cost-free passive symmetry verification filter, automatically rejecting projective outcomes corrupted by single-qubit bit-flip (XX) errors without ancilla overhead.

These findings suggest several concrete directions for quantum hardware co-design, algorithmic scaling, and near-term implementation: (1) Qubit Connectivity and Routing: While next-nearest-neighbor J2J_{2} couplings require routing SWAP networks on fixed planar superconducting topologies, platforms featuring reconfigurable or all-to-all connectivity—such as neutral-atom optical tweezer arrays and trapped-ion shuttling architectures—can implement J2J_{2} interactions natively, substantially reducing two-qubit gate overhead. (2) Measurement Optimization and Gradient Scaling: In the Hamiltonian Variational Ansatz, total measurement overhead scales as 𝒪⁡(Nθ⋅L⋅Nshots)\mathcal{O}(N_{\theta}\cdot L\cdot N_{\text{shots}}). To mitigate measurement burdens and gradient variance decay on large lattices, advanced measurement protocols—such as grouped commuting Pauli measurements and localized subsystem shadow tomography [14, 15]—can extract multi-qubit expectation values and evaluate deflation overlap penalties from few-body marginals that retain non-vanishing gradient variances [3]. (3) Hybrid Adaptive Circuits and Warm-Starting: While shallow HVAs with local observables evade untargeted Barren plateaus [3, 26], scaling deep into p≫Lp\gg L or 2D geometries risks entanglement-induced gradient suppression: Var​[∂θkℒ]∼𝒪⁡(2−L)\text{Var}[\partial_{\theta_{k}}\mathcal{L}]\sim\mathcal{O}(2^{-L}). Combining fixed-depth ansätze with symmetry-preserving ADAPT-VQE [11] and classical warm-starting via shallow Matrix Product States (MPS) [49] provides viable pathways to place initial parameters within the convex basin, ensuring efficient optimization beyond one dimension.

In broader context, the Dual Spin-Sector paradigm is directly applicable beyond one dimension to frustrated two-dimensional geometries, such as the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} square lattice, triangular, and kagome antiferromagnets [8, 28]. In these systems, competing exchange pathways generate quantum spin liquid phases, valence-bond crystals, and subtle singlet-triplet ordering crossovers that pose formidable challenges for classical tensor networks and quantum Monte Carlo. By exploiting exact non-Abelian spin symmetries to partition optimization across magnetization sectors, this framework provides a practical, resource-efficient blueprint for exploring frustrated quantum magnetism on intermediate-scale quantum devices.
